Reading walking speed from the scalp

the idea

The idea, and the catch

Take EEG recorded while people walk at three speeds. Cut it into short windows, measure how much power sits in each frequency band, and train a model to name the speed. It is a clean little project and the pipeline works fine.

The trouble is the first number it gives you. I got 0.923, and that number is close to meaningless.

Each one minute recording gets cut into 58 windows that overlap each other by half. Shuffle those windows and deal them into a training set and a test set, and windows from the same recording land on both sides. They share half their samples, so they are near enough copies. The model can score well by recognising a window it has already seen most of. It never has to learn anything about walking.

how the data is split

The split is the whole experiment

Same model, same features, same scoring. The only thing that changes is where the line between training and testing gets drawn.

Balanced accuracy under three ways of splitting.
how the split is drawn scorewhat it tells you
at random across windows 0.923 very little, for the reason above
by recording 0.333 something worse than nothing, see below
by person 0.528 whether it works on somebody new

This is a known trap rather than a clever discovery. Leinonen and colleagues found the same thing in heart recordings [11]. Ordinary cross validation gave scores that were too high, and holding out whole sources gave honest ones.

a second problem

The features know who you are

The middle row of that table bothered me for a while. Splitting by recording is a weaker rule than splitting by person, so it ought to score higher. It sits at chance instead.

So I ran the obvious check. Instead of asking the model to name the speed, I asked it to name the person. Out of 58 people it picked the right one 0.568 of the time, against a chance level of 1.7 percent. That is about 33 times better than guessing.

Everybody walked all three speeds once. Hold out one of their recordings and the model has already been trained on the other two, so it knows what that person looks like at the two speeds it has seen, and it files the held out recording under one of those. The right answer is the one speed it was never shown. Real 1.0 m/s ends up called 0.75 m/s more often than it gets called correctly.

That people can be picked out from their EEG is not news. It was shown back in 2007 [9] and there is a whole survey of the field [10]. What is worth saying here is that the personal signature is strong enough to drown out the thing I was trying to measure, and that it drags the score below chance rather than above it.

Splitting by person is the only version that answers the question a real device would face. Everything after this uses it.

before any model

What is in the signal

It is worth looking at the spectra before letting a model summarise them for you. Two things climb with walking speed and both are visible by eye.

Power goes up at every frequency as people walk faster, so this is a rise in the overall level rather than a shift between bands. And below about 10 Hz there is a row of sharp spikes: the step rhythm and its multiples, pressed into the EEG by the head bobbing. Measured off the muscle recordings, the step rate runs 0.50 m/s gives 0.68 Hz, 0.75 m/s gives 0.81 Hz, 1.00 m/s gives 0.91 Hz.

holding out one person at a time

Brain, muscle, and both

The dataset also carries muscle recordings from twelve leg muscles, which makes the honest comparison possible. How much of this comes from the brain, and how much from the legs doing the walking?

All three run on the same rows, 8112 windows from 166 recordings, so they can be compared directly. A model that guesses at random scores 0.330 here, which is the check that the folds are built properly.

Held out one person at a time, 57 people.
signalseach window whole recordingkappa rank correlation
brain0.727 0.915 0.589 0.733
muscle0.893 0.963 0.840 0.914
both 0.899 0.976 0.848 0.920

Muscle beats brain by a wide margin, and putting brain signals on top of muscle buys almost nothing. Tortora and colleagues built a gait decoder in 2020 that combined the two and did get a gain from it [6]. I do not see one that size here.

The whole recording column is the number worth quoting for a device. A chair would not act on a single two second window. It would gather a few seconds and then decide.

Calibration matters more than which signal you pick

There are two ways a device could meet somebody new. It could work straight out of the box, or it could record them for a minute first and use that to set its own baseline. The second version scales each feature against the spread of that person's own recordings. It never sees their labels.

signalsno calibration with calibration
brain 0.554 0.723
muscle 0.681 0.889
both 0.726 0.889

Taking away each person's baseline is worth more than switching from brain to muscle. There is a catch and it is a real one. The calibration step uses the held out person's own recordings, including the ones being tested. So it describes a device that gets a calibration session, and it does not describe one that works cold.

These rows use only the people who also have muscle recordings, which is why the no calibration brain score here is 0.554 rather than the 0.528 quoted earlier on the full set.

shuffled labels

Could this just be luck?

To find out I shuffled the speed labels inside each person, so everybody keeps their three recordings and only the name on each one gets swapped around. Then I ran the whole thing again 200 times. Shuffling across everyone at once would also wreck the person structure, which would make the comparison too easy and the answer too flattering.

Real scores against 200 shuffled runs.
signalsreal score shuffled averageshuffled 95th p
brain0.7190.3330.370below 0.005
muscle0.8870.3330.388below 0.005
both0.8870.3320.383below 0.005

The shuffled runs land on chance. That is the more useful half of this test. If the way I split the data were leaking anywhere, the shuffled runs would sit above chance too, and they do not.

taking shortcuts away

What the model is actually reading

Walking faster means stepping faster. Step rhythm turns up in the brain recording because the head bobs and the neck muscles work, so the worry is that the model is reading footsteps off the scalp. To test it I took away one suspected shortcut at a time and trained again.

Each row removes one thing, with calibration on.
what the model gets numbersscore
everything209 0.738
alpha, beta and gamma only, as the video asks 114 0.723
delta and theta gone, where the step rhythm lives 133 0.727
total power only, no frequency detail at all 19 0.692
front and side electrodes gone 143 0.735
C3, Cz and C4 only, over the motor strip 33 0.655

Taking out the bands that hold the step rhythm barely dents the score. And total power on its own, 19 numbers with no frequency detail in them, gets to 0.692. So the model is mostly reading a rise in the overall level rather than a change in the shape of the spectrum.

For a while I read this the friendly way

Shuffling one electrode's features at a time and watching the score drop gives this:

electrodes average drop each
C3, Cz, C4, over the motor strip 0.0162
the other ten 0.0106
Fp1, Fp2, F7, F8, T7, T8, nearest the eyes and neck 0.0031

The electrodes closest to the eyes and the neck muscles turn out to be the least useful. The motor strip electrodes are the most useful, and beta is the strongest band at 0.052. Beta over the motor strip is a normal thing to see during movement [7][12], so this looked like real brain activity to me.

Then I found a paper that says otherwise

Nordin, Hairston and Ferris published a study in 2019 that lands straight on this question [2]. They built a two layer electrode, where one layer sits on the scalp and a second layer sits on top of it, wired separately, picking up movement only. That gave them a recording of the artifact by itself, which they could then subtract. Their people walked at 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 m/s, so their two slowest speeds are my two extremes.

Two of their findings matter here. Once the artifact was taken out, alpha and beta power over sensorimotor cortex went down as people walked faster. And the movement recordings, along with the neck muscle recordings, showed broad power going up at faster speeds.

In my data, alpha and beta at C3, Cz and C4 go up by +6.5 dB on average between 0.5 and 1.0 m/s, and the rise is broad across the whole band. That is the same direction as their movement channel and the opposite direction from their cleaned brain signal. So the friendly reading does not hold up. What my model is using looks like the artifact they measured rather than the cortex they measured.

One thing does survive. Fp1 and Fp2 sit just above the eyes, which is where blink artifact turns up first, and they hardly change with speed. They were also the two least useful electrodes. So I can rule out eye blinks as the main source. Neck muscle and head movement do not stay near the front of the head, so ruling out blinks rules out very little.

The field does not agree on how bad this problem is. Nathan and Contreras-Vidal reported in 2016 that motion did not affect scalp EEG much during treadmill walking, with a warning once speed gets near 4.5 km/h [3]. My fastest condition is 3.6 km/h, under that line, which would put me in the clear on their account. Jacobsen and colleagues reached a less comfortable answer in 2020 and described clear gait related artifacts in mobile EEG [4]. Gorjan and colleagues wrote guidelines in 2022 that treat movement artifact as a problem needing active removal [5]. My results sit with the second group.

Window length is not doing the work

Two second windows were an arbitrary pick, so I ran the whole comparison again at four seconds. Brain signals gain about four points, which is what a noisy measurement should do when you hand it twice as much data. Muscle stays put. Brain is the weakest of the three either way.

signals2 second windows4 second windows
brain0.7230.769
muscle0.8890.884
both0.8890.899

interactive, runs in your browser

Try it yourself

Scores on shuffled windows are not what a device lives through. So here is the model driving a chair. I took one person out of the training set, S44, joined their three recordings end to end, and fed them through the model one window at a time. I picked the person whose score sits closest to the middle of the group rather than the best one.

The dots are the raw guesses, one a second, straight from the model. The dark line is the real treadmill speed. The blue line is what the chair would actually be told after smoothing. Drag the sliders and the two sets of signals behave in opposite ways, which is the whole point of putting this here.

Wheelchair speed controller

Real model output for person S44, who was never in the training set. Only the smoothing is redone here.

Signals used
5 windows
2 windows

real treadmill speed what the chair is told raw guess, once a second speed change

0% command right
0 s time to settle
0.50 m/s chair told to go

Time to settle is how long after a speed change the command reaches the new speed and stays there.

With muscle in the mix the raw guesses are already right almost every second, so smoothing buys nothing and costs delay. At no smoothing the command is right 98.6 percent of the time and settles in one second. Wind the slider up to fifteen and that falls to 89.2 percent and eight seconds. The best thing you can do is leave it alone.

Brain signals alone do the reverse. The guesses jump around so much that at light settings the command never holds still at all, which is why the settling time sits above thirty seconds. You have to average over about twelve seconds before it stops flipping. That gets the command right 90.5 percent of the time, but by then the chair is reacting to what you wanted twelve seconds ago. There is no setting on this slider that gives you a command which is both steady and quick.

The settings used in the write-up: smoothing of 5, hold of 2.
signalsraw windows right command right time to settle
brain only75.7%88.5%33 s, 38 s
brain and muscle97.3%95.9%3 s, 3 s

The command right column makes the brain only model look usable and the settling column shows that it is not. It does reach the right speed, then drops back to the wrong one for a few seconds, over and over. For a chair, settling time is the number that decides whether you could ride it.

honest limits

What this does not show

The recording order cannot be undone

Every person walked 0.5, then 0.75, then 1.0, in one sitting with the headset fitted once. Speed lines up exactly with time since the session started, and so does everything that drifts with it: the dry electrodes settling in, sweat, hair moving, getting tired. No amount of analysis on this dataset pulls those apart. Settling it needs a study that varies the order between people.

Most of the signal is probably movement

The comparison with Nordin and colleagues points that way, and I have no way to strip the artifact properly without the two layer hardware they used.

The calibrated numbers use the test person's own data

No labels, but still their data. Read them as the score for a device that gets a calibration session first.

The group is narrow

Fifty-eight healthy adults with an average age of 24, on a treadmill, at three slow speeds. People who use wheelchairs are not this group, and a treadmill is not a pavement.

This is not a brain-computer interface

The people in this dataset were walking. Somebody who needs a powered chair is not. Reading an intended speed off somebody sitting still is a much harder problem and nothing here shows it can be done. Reviews of EEG control for lower limb assistive robots give a sense of how far off that is [8].

the small print

Notes, privacy and terms

Privacy

This is a single static page. It has no accounts, no forms, no comments and no analytics.

What the page collects

Nothing. There is no tracking code on it, no analytics script and no advertising. It does not ask you for anything and it has nowhere to send anything.

What the page loads

Everything the page needs is inside the file you are reading. The fonts, the charts and the model output are all embedded, so opening the page makes no request to any other company's servers. Nobody learns that you read it except the service hosting it.

What the host can see

Whoever hosts this page can keep ordinary server records, such as the address your request came from, in the same way any website host can. That sits outside this page and is covered by the host's own privacy policy rather than this one.

About the people in the data

The recordings come from a public dataset that its authors anonymised before release, under an approved ethics protocol at their university. It holds no names, no contact details and nothing that identifies a participant. Nothing on this page can be traced back to an individual who took part.

Questions

If you want something on this page corrected or removed, contact whoever sent you the link.

Cookies and storage

This page sets no cookies. It writes nothing to local storage or session storage, and it stores nothing else on your device.

The short notice near the top of the page disappears when you dismiss it, and that choice is not saved anywhere. Reload the page and the notice comes back, because nothing was written down.

The interactive controller runs entirely in your browser using data that is already inside the page. It sends nothing out and saves nothing.

Because no cookies are set and nothing is stored, there is nothing here for you to consent to or opt out of. If the service hosting this page sets its own cookies, those are covered by that service's policy.

Terms of use

This is a student project written to learn and to be looked at. It is offered as is, with no warranty of any kind, and no promise that anything on it is correct or fit for any purpose.

Not medical or clinical advice

Nothing here is medical advice. None of this is a medical device or part of one. Do not use anything on this page, or the code behind it, to make a decision about anybody's care, treatment, mobility equipment or safety. The wheelchair framing is a way of explaining the problem. The model shown here is nowhere near fit to steer a real chair, and the page says why.

Limits

To the fullest extent the law allows, the author is not liable for any loss or damage arising from use of this page, the figures on it or the code behind it.

The data

The recordings belong to Katmah and colleagues and are published on PhysioNet under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence, which allows reuse with credit. The dataset itself is not redistributed here. Credit is given in the references, and anyone reusing this work should credit them too.

This page and the code

The text, figures and code written by me are released under the MIT licence. You may reuse them with credit. The findings are reported as I measured them, and the limits section is part of the finding rather than a disclaimer bolted on the end.

Accessibility

I aimed at WCAG 2.1 level AA. Here is what that meant in practice and where it falls short, so you can judge for yourself.

What is in place

  • A skip link to the main text, and proper landmarks for header, navigation, main content and footer.
  • Headings run in order without skipping levels, so a screen reader can move through the page by structure.
  • Every control in the interactive section is a standard HTML input or button, so it works with a keyboard and with assistive software. Focus is always visible.
  • Body text meets a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background in both the light and the dark theme. Small grey captions were darkened until they passed.
  • Every figure has a text description that says what it shows, and the finding in each figure is also written out in the surrounding text, so nothing is only available as a picture.
  • The page respects a reduced motion setting. The moving line drawing at the top freezes and the demo does not animate.
  • Text reflows down to a 320 pixel wide screen and at 200 percent zoom. Wide tables and figures scroll inside their own box rather than pushing the page sideways.
  • Colour is never the only way information is given. Numbers are written out next to every coloured bar.

Known gaps

  • The charts are images produced by a plotting library, so they cannot be read line by line by a screen reader. The description and the surrounding text carry the same information.
  • The moving line drawing at the top is decoration and is hidden from screen readers on purpose. It shows nothing that is not written in the text beside it.
  • The interactive chart is drawn on a canvas, which screen readers cannot inspect. A written summary sits next to it and updates as you change the settings, giving the same numbers.

Telling me about a problem

If part of this page does not work with the software you use, contact whoever sent you the link and say what failed. That is the fastest way to get it fixed.
